items.title: The Desktop I Wanted Didn't Exist... So I Built It
items.description: Three years in the making, this is the Linux desktop I use every day. Built around DWM, Quickshell, and a Fedora base, it brings together tiling windows, matching themes, display profiles, Bluetooth, audio, and system updates with minimal dependencies. I'll walk through the setup, demonstrate a fresh installation, and show how I configure shortcuts, window rules, and layouts without recompiling DWM. I'll also explain why I moved from Arch to Fedora and why I'm still using X11. This is a personal project in beta, with rough edges still to polish. Take what you like, customize it, or build something of your own. items.title: Is AI Doom Real... or Just Good Marketing?
items.description: Is AI doom about protecting the public, protecting profits, or a little of both? I break down the incentives behind AI fear, why companies like OpenAI and Anthropic might welcome regulation, and how cheaper open-weight and local models could challenge their business models. We also look at real AI risks, questions about independent evaluations, and why an AI bubble bursting could hurt far more than tech companies. Some of these connections are speculation, not proven facts, but they're worth examining alongside the doom-and-gloom headlines. Do you think AI regulation will protect users or protect the biggest companies? Let me know in the comments. items.title: Omarchy: Arch Savior or Overhyped Reskin?
items.description: Everyone seems to be hyping Omarchy. I'm not switching to it, but some of its ideas are absolutely worth stealing. In this hands-on review, I dig into DHH's take on Arch Linux and Hyprland: the plugins, polished theming, helpful menus, and opinionated defaults. I cover what impressed me, what I'd remove, and why my own desktop takes a different direction. Then I show my Fedora setup with DWM, X11, and Quickshell, including the ideas Omarchy inspired me to bring into my own workflow. That's the beauty of Linux: keep what you like, change what you don't, and build something that works for YOU. Which Omarchy feature would you steal for your own desktop? Let me know in the comments. items.title: I Rebuilt My Entire Website in Astro… Was It Worth It?
items.description: I rebuilt my entire website from Hugo to Astro after years of using Hugo as the backbone of ChrisTitus.com. Hugo was fast, simple, and honestly still fantastic—but my site had grown into much more than a blog. Downloads, livestream archives, chat replay, forums, search, store integrations, and other features were starting to push Hugo beyond what I wanted it to do. In this video, I break down why I moved to Astro, what the massive migration looked like, how I used AI review loops to help with the conversion, and what Astro gives me that Hugo didn't. I also cover the downsides: Astro has a much heavier Node/npm ecosystem, requires more security and CI checks, and the migration even appears to have reduced my AdSense revenue. Was it worth it? For my site, absolutely. But if you're running a straightforward static blog, I'd still recommend Hugo. Thanks to Blacksmith for sponsoring this video. I’ve been using their GitHub Actions runners and caching to significantly reduce CI build times. https://link.christitus.com/blacksmith **Chapters** 00:00 Why Leave Hugo? 02:02 The Astro Migration 04:31 Why Astro Wins 07:27 CI & Security 09:11 Was It Worth It? ►► Digital Downloads ➜ https://www.cttstore.com ►► Patreon ➜ https://www.patreon.com/christitustech ►► Twitch ➜ https://www.twitch.tv/christitustech ►► Website and Guides ➜ https://christitus.com

items.title: GitHub Copilot App Is Actually Good… Just Not with Copilot
items.description: GitHub Copilot is actually a surprisingly good GitHub app… once you stop thinking of it as Copilot. In this video, I show how I’m using the GitHub Copilot desktop app on Linux as a dashboard for managing repositories, issues, pull requests, notifications, and daily triage across a massive number of projects. I’ll also show how I bypass the built-in Copilot subscription and connect my existing OpenAI Codex subscription through CLIProxyAPI, giving me one AI subscription that I can use across multiple applications. For developers managing dozens or even hundreds of repositories, this has become a surprisingly useful way to prioritize issues, organize PRs, keep local repositories synchronized, and figure out what actually needs attention. Article link: https://christitus.com/github-copilot-on-linux/ Thanks to Blacksmith for sponsoring this video. items.title: I Finally Built the Impossible Windows App
items.description: After 3 years of development, the project I thought might be impossible is finally here. I completely rebuilt my Windows Utility as a native .NET application while keeping compatibility with the open-source WinUtil configuration. Instead of simply executing PowerShell behind the scenes, it translates those tweaks into native .NET implementations. That means faster execution, better system detection, automatic updates, localization, restore points, Windows tweaking, app installs, and an insanely fast Windows 11 ISO creator. If you've previously purchased the Windows Utility, you get this new version and future updates. items.title: My AI Coding Workflow That Actually Works
items.description: Most people use AI coding agents by giving them one giant prompt and letting them run wild. That might work for a tiny project, but it quickly falls apart when you are building real software. In this video, I walk through my complete AI development workflow using agents, specifications, roadmaps, testing, pull requests, CI, security scanning, and independent code reviews. I also demonstrate the process on a real project, from the initial request through review, fixes, validation, and the final merge. The model matters, but your workflow matters more. Manual gates, clear acceptance criteria, small pull requests, and proper testing are what turn AI-generated code into maintainable software. What does your AI development workflow look like? Let me know what you would add or change. items.title: I Spent 1.5 Billion AI Tokens on Absolute Slop
items.description: I spent 1.5 billion AI tokens and roughly 24 hours of compute trying to expand a real .NET application. The result was nearly 170,000 lines of bloated, unmaintainable code that ultimately had to be thrown away. In this video, I break down where the project went wrong, why a more powerful model would not have solved the underlying problem, and how developers should actually use AI on large software projects. AI is an incredible pair programmer, debugger, and productivity tool. But without proper architecture, checkpoints, Git, and someone who understands the code, it can generate technical debt faster than any human developer. What do you think? Is AI coding getting better, or are we just producing slop faster? **Chapters** 00:00 1.5 Billion Tokens 03:17 170,000 Lines 06:37 Technical Debt 09:45 Resetting Everything 13:06 The Right Approach 16:06 Final Verdict ►► Digital Downloads ➜ https://www.cttstore.com ►► Patreon ➜ https://www.patreon.com/christitustech ►► Twitch ➜ https://www.twitch.tv/christitustech ►► Website and Guides ➜ https://christitus.com

items.title: 10 Projects AI is Good At
items.description: What can AI ACTUALLY do? Here is what I've built with it in the past month. I built a searchable gaming guide, automated Fedora package repository, website moderation dashboard, custom Linux desktop, cross-platform fitness tracker, and a self-hosted open-source alternative to QuickBooks. These aren’t disposable demos or AI slop. They are real projects designed to solve problems in my work and personal life. In this video, I show what AI development looks like when you combine capable models with Git, testing, code review, documentation, guardrails, and a solid technical foundation. items.title: I Quit Arch Linux After 794 Days (Here's Why)
items.description: After 794 days on Arch Linux, I'm switching to Fedora — and it has nothing to do with the recent AUR compromise. Here's why constant rolling-release updates became a productivity killer, and how I built my own minimal Fedora spin with DWM and QuickShell to replace it. In this video I cover: - Why the AUR "hack" panic is overblown - How Arch was costing me dev time - Why I picked Fedora over Debian - My custom DWM + QuickShell setup - Fedora's SELinux & FirewallD defaults - Why I'm building my own Fedora ISO - Red Hat's CentOS/Rocky history - Final thoughts on Arch vs Fedora 🔗 Full writeup: https://christitus.com/switch-from-arch-to-fedora/ CHAPTERS: 00:00 The AUR Scare 01:19 Why I'm Switching 01:57 Dev Over Content 02:19 Arch Breaks Often 03:09 AUR Best Practices 05:29 Only Three Distros 07:25 My DWM Setup 09:41 Arch Still Rules 11:04 My Fedora Spin 13:46 Final Thoughts #Linux #Fedora #ArchLinux #DWM #Homelab #OpenSource ►► Digital Downloads ➜ https://www.cttstore.com ►► Patreon ➜ https://www.patreon.com/christitustech ►► Twitch ➜ https://www.twitch.tv/christitustech ►► Website and Guides ➜ https://christitus.com

items.title: DaVinci Resolve on Linux: Fix EVERY Common Issue
items.description: DaVinci Resolve on Linux is powerful but notoriously finicky — Blackmagic builds it for RHEL-based distros like Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux, which means modern distros like Arch and Ubuntu run into library mismatches, GPU detection problems, missing codecs, and broken fonts right out of the box. In this video, I walk through every major issue I've run into running Resolve on Linux for years, and exactly how I fixed each one. I cover my Resolve-Linux repo and the resolve-fix script that solves library mismatches by forcing Resolve to use your system's newer libraries instead of the outdated ones it ships with. I also go over GPU setup for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel (including my Intel Arc B70 setup), the FFmpeg encoder plugin for H.264/H.265 codec support on the free version, my resolve-convert script for batch re-encoding footage to DNxHR, and the Fusion path map fix for fonts that won't show up in your titles. If you're serious about editing video on Linux, Resolve is leagues ahead of free alternatives like Kdenlive — you just need to know these fixes first. 🔧 Tools & Scripts mentioned: Resolve-Linux repo & resolve-fix script - https://github.com/ChrisTitusTech/resolve-linux FFmpeg encoder plugin (AUR) - https://github.com/EdvinNilsson/ffmpeg_encoder_plugin _Note:_ FFMPEG encoder is just ENCODING to h264/h265 NOT Decoding! 👍 Let me know in the comments which Resolve-on-Linux issue you've run into — I bet it falls into one of these buckets! 0:00 Intro 0:35 Linux Distro Choice 1:27 Common Resolve Issues 2:08 FFmpeg Codec Plugin 2:32 Fixing Library Mismatch 4:12 GPU Driver Setup 5:18 Codec Workaround Script 7:27 Audio-Only Re-Encode 7:45 Missing Fonts Fix 9:18 Backup Script 9:44 Final Thoughts ►► Digital Downloads ➜ https://www.cttstore.com ►► Patreon ➜ https://www.patreon.com/christitustech ►► Twitch ➜ https://www.twitch.tv/christitustech ►► Website and Guides ➜ https://christitus.com
